keyTakeaways: Third party insurance is legal minimum, but comprehensive is often only £10-20/month more and worth it for touring
Your postcode and bike storage location affect premiums more than almost any other factor – garage storage can save 20-30%
Always declare modifications and mileage accurately to avoid invalidating your policy when you need to claim
No-claims bonus is gold – avoid small claims to protect it and save up to 50% on premiums after five years
Sports-styled 125s cost significantly more to insure than commuter-style bikes, even with identical performance
Shop around every year before renewal – loyalty to insurers doesn't pay, you'll almost always find cheaper quotes elsewhere

faq.q: Do I need insurance if I'm only riding a 125cc on a CBT?
faq.a: Yes, absolutely. All motorcycles ridden on UK public roads require at least third party insurance, regardless of engine size or licence type. Riding without insurance is illegal and can result in hefty fines, points on your licence, and bike seizure.

faq.q: Is comprehensive insurance cheaper than third party for 125cc bikes?
faq.a: Sometimes, yes. Insurers often price comprehensive cover lower because riders who choose it tend to be more careful and make fewer claims. Always compare both to find the best deal for your situation.

faq.q: Will passing my full motorcycle test reduce my 125cc insurance?
faq.a: Usually yes, but not dramatically. You'll see some reduction when moving from CBT to a full licence, but the biggest savings come from building up years of no-claims bonus and getting older.

faq.q: Do I need to tell my insurer about bar-end mirrors or a phone mount?
faq.a: Technically, any modification should be declared. Bar-end mirrors definitely need declaring as they replace standard equipment. Phone mounts are grey area but better to mention them. Failing to declare mods can invalidate your entire policy.

faq.q: Can I ride my 125cc in Europe on UK insurance?
faq.a: Most UK policies include basic third-party cover for EU travel, but you'll typically need to pay extra (usually £20-40) for comprehensive cover abroad. Always contact your insurer before travelling to arrange proper cover.

faq.q: How much does security equipment reduce insurance costs?
faq.a: Sold Secure approved locks and alarms can reduce premiums by 10-20% with most insurers. Combined with garage storage, you could save 30-40% compared to street parking with no security. Always keep receipts to prove you own the equipment.

content:
125cc Bike Insurance: What You Actually Need to Know in 2026

Right, let's talk about 125cc insurance. I know it's not the most exciting topic when you're dreaming about riding the NC500 or exploring the Peak District, but getting your insurance sorted properly can save you hundreds of quid and a whole lot of hassle down the line. I've been riding 125s for years – they're brilliant little machines for UK touring when you know how to work them – and I've learned a fair bit about the insurance game along the way.

Whether you're a new rider on a CBT or you're choosing a 125 for economical touring around Britain, insurance is one of those things you need to get right from the start. So grab a brew, and let me walk you through everything I've learned about insuring these smaller bikes in 2026.

Why 125cc Insurance Is Different

First things first: 125cc insurance isn't just "cheaper bike insurance." It's a completely different beast, and insurers look at it through a very specific lens. Most 125 riders fall into one of two camps – either you're a younger or newer rider on a CBT, or you're an experienced rider who's chosen a 125 for practical or economic reasons. The insurers know this, and they price accordingly.

I've ridden my Yamaha YS125 from Cornwall up to the Scottish Highlands, and the insurance on that little bike has been one of the best investments I've made. But here's the thing: the same bike can cost wildly different amounts to insure depending on how you present yourself and what cover you choose.

The CBT Factor

If you're riding on a CBT (Compulsory Basic Training), insurers see you as higher risk. That's just the reality. You haven't passed your full test, and statistically, CBT riders have more accidents. I'm not saying that's you – but that's how the numbers work. When I first started out on a CBT back in the day, my insurance was nearly £800 for a tatty old CG125. These days in 2026, you're looking at similar or even higher figures if you're young and in a city.

But here's what I learned: your postcode matters more than almost anything else. When I moved from South London to rural Derbyshire, my premium dropped by nearly 40%. If you're able to store your bike in a garage or secure compound rather than on the street, tell your insurer. It makes a real difference.

Types of Cover: What Do You Actually Need?

Let's break down the three main types of insurance, because there's a lot of confusion about what you really need versus what's nice to have.

Third Party Only (TPO)

This is the legal minimum in the UK. It covers damage and injury you cause to other people and their property, but nothing for your bike or yourself. I've used TPO on older 125s that were worth less than £500. If your bike gets nicked or you drop it, you're paying for repairs yourself.

Here's my rule: if your bike is worth less than about £800 and you could afford to replace it without financial hardship, TPO might make sense. But remember, even a minor claim against you for damaging someone's car could run into thousands.

Third Party, Fire and Theft (TPFT)

This adds protection if your bike is stolen or burns out. Given that 125s are among the most commonly nicked bikes in Britain – especially in cities – I almost always recommend at least TPFT. I've had mates lose Honda CB125Fs and Yamaha YZF-R125s to thieves in Manchester and Birmingham. Without theft cover, they were out of pocket entirely.

The extra cost over TPO is usually pretty minimal, often £50-100 a year. For that peace of mind when you're parked up at a cafe on the Island to Highlands route, it's worth it.

Fully Comprehensive

Fully comp covers everything: damage to your bike, theft, fire, and third-party claims. Surprisingly, fully comp is sometimes cheaper than TPFT because insurers know that riders who choose comprehensive cover tend to be more careful. I've seen this with my own quotes.

If you're touring on your 125 – and yes, you absolutely can tour on a 125 – fully comp is what I'd recommend. When you're out on the A470 through Snowdonia in typical Welsh drizzle, or navigating the twisty bits of the A537 Cat and Fiddle, accidents can happen even to careful riders. Comprehensive cover means you can focus on enjoying the ride rather than worrying about every potential hazard.

The difference between third party and comprehensive on a 125 is often less than a tenner a month, but the peace of mind when you're miles from home in the Lake District is priceless.

What Affects Your 125cc Insurance Premium

Right, let's get into the nitty-gritty of what actually moves the needle on your insurance costs. Understanding these factors has saved me hundreds over the years.

Age and Experience

This is the big one. If you're under 25, expect to pay significantly more. When I was 21, I was paying nearly three times what I pay now in my thirties for essentially the same bike. There's not much you can do about your age, but you can build up your no-claims bonus as quickly as possible.

Once you pass your full motorcycle test (A1, A2, or A licence), tell your insurer immediately. It should reduce your premium, though not as dramatically as you might hope. The real savings come with years of claim-free riding.

Where You Live and Store Your Bike

I've touched on this already, but it bears repeating: postcode is massive. Urban postcodes, particularly in London, Manchester, Birmingham, and Liverpool, attract the highest premiums because that's where most thefts and accidents happen.

Storage is equally important. Here's what I've learned:

  • Locked garage: Best option, can reduce premiums by 20-30%
  • Secured compound or driveway: Better than street parking, around 10-15% reduction
  • Street parking with security devices: Better than nothing, but still expensive in cities
  • Street parking with no security: Expect the highest premiums and possible excess requirements

I always use a disc lock with an alarm plus a chain when I'm touring and stopping overnight. Not only does this help with security, but many insurers offer discounts for Sold Secure approved locks. Pick up quality gear from SportsBikeShop and keep your receipts – you'll need to prove you're using them.

Your Mileage

Be honest about your annual mileage, but don't overestimate. If you genuinely only ride 2,000 miles a year for commuting and the odd weekend ride, say so. But if you're like me and you're planning to rack up 8,000+ miles touring around Britain, you need to declare that accurately.

I once underestimated my mileage to save a few quid, then had to make a claim. The insurer checked my MOT records, saw the discrepancy, and nearly refused the claim. Not worth the risk.

Bike Modifications

Even minor mods need to be declared. That aftermarket exhaust that makes your bike sound better? Tell your insurer. The slightly sportier mirrors? Declare them. Bar-end indicators? Yep, those too.

Some modifications won't affect your premium, but failing to declare them can invalidate your entire policy. I learned this the hard way when I fitted heated grips to my old 125 and didn't update my policy. Fortunately, I didn't need to claim, but it was a lesson learned.

Getting the Best Price: My Practical Tips

After years of insuring various 125s, here's what actually works to reduce your premium without compromising your cover.

Use Comparison Sites – But Not Only Comparison Sites

Start with the big comparison sites (Compare the Market, Go Compare, Confused.com), but don't stop there. Some specialist motorcycle insurers like Bennetts, Carole Nash, and Lexham don't appear on all comparison sites. I always get quotes from at least 2-3 comparison sites plus a couple of direct insurers.

Set aside a couple of hours to do this properly. The cheapest quote isn't always the best – read the policy details, check the excess amounts, and look at what's actually covered.

Pay Annually If You Can

Monthly payments are convenient, but you'll typically pay 15-20% more over the year due to interest. If you can scrape together the money to pay annually, do it. I know it hurts handing over £600 in one go, but it's better than paying £700+ over twelve months.

Build Your No-Claims Bonus

Every year you ride without making a claim, your premium should drop. After five years of no-claims, you can often get discounts of 50% or more. Guard this bonus jealously.

Here's a tip: if you have a minor drop or damage that'll cost £400 to fix and your excess is £350, pay for it yourself rather than claiming. You'll save money in the long run by keeping your no-claims intact.

Consider Advanced Rider Training

Taking an advanced riding course like IAM RoadSmart or BikeSafe can reduce your premiums with some insurers. Plus, it makes you a better, safer rider. I did my IAM Advanced Rider course a few years back, and not only did my insurance drop, but I genuinely enjoy riding more now. The skills I learned make touring on smaller bikes much more enjoyable, especially on challenging roads like the Hardknott Pass or the Applecross coastal road.

Choose Your Bike Wisely

Not all 125s are equal in the eyes of insurers. Sports-styled bikes like the Yamaha YZF-R125 or the Honda CBR125R typically cost more to insure than more sedate machines like the Honda CB125F or Suzuki VanVan.

If insurance cost is a major concern, consider a less sporty model. You might miss out on some street cred, but you'll save money and still have a bike that can handle proper British touring. I've ridden the A9 through the Scottish Highlands on a basic commuter-style 125, and it was brilliant.

Multi-Bike Policies and Touring Cover

If you're like me and you've got more than one bike (I currently run a 125 for local stuff and a bigger bike for longer tours), ask about multi-bike policies. Some insurers will give you significant discounts for insuring multiple bikes with them.

European Cover for Cross-Channel Tours

Planning to ride your 125 to France or Belgium? Most UK policies include basic third-party cover for EU travel, but you'll often need to pay extra for comprehensive cover abroad. In 2026, even post-Brexit, this is usually pretty straightforward – just call your insurer and arrange it before you travel.

I took my 125 across to Normandy a couple of years back, and the extra cover cost me about £25 for two weeks. Well worth it for peace of mind on foreign roads.

Common Mistakes That'll Cost You

Let me share some cock-ups I've made or seen others make, so you can avoid them:

  • Not updating your address: If you move house and don't tell your insurer, your policy could be invalid
  • Lending your bike to mates: Check if your policy covers other riders. Many don't, or require them to be named
  • Using your bike for food delivery without business cover: Social, domestic and pleasure plus commuting doesn't cover commercial use. You'll need special cover for delivery work
  • Automatic renewal without shopping around: Loyalty doesn't pay in insurance. Your renewal quote is almost always higher than what you can get elsewhere
  • Cancelling mid-term without checking: Cancellation fees can be brutal, sometimes 40-50% of your premium

What to Do After You Buy Your Policy

Once you've got your insurance sorted, don't just file away the documents and forget about them. Here's what I do:

Save your insurance certificate and schedule somewhere accessible – I keep photos on my phone and physical copies in my touring luggage. If you get stopped by police, you'll need to produce these within seven days.

Set a calendar reminder for about three weeks before your renewal date. This gives you time to shop around without the panic of last-minute renewal.

Keep a record of any modifications you make to your bike. Take photos with dates. If you ever need to claim, having this documentation makes the process much smoother.

If you're planning a big tour – say, riding the full North Coast 500 or a multi-day expedition through Wales – use our trip planning tool to map out your route and accommodation. Then make sure your insurance covers you for the full duration and distance.

Looking Ahead: Insurance Trends in 2026

The insurance market keeps evolving. In 2026, we're seeing more insurers offering black-box or telematics policies for 125cc bikes. These track your riding style and can offer discounts for smooth, safe riding. I'm not personally a fan of being monitored, but if you're a new rider with a clean record, these policies can save you serious money.

Electric 125s are also becoming more common, and insurance for these is often cheaper than petrol equivalents. If you're considering an electric 125 for touring around Britain, the lower insurance costs are another tick in their favour, alongside the running cost savings.

Final Thoughts: Just Get On With It

Look, I know insurance isn't fun. It's not why we ride. But spending a few hours getting your 125cc insurance sorted properly means you can focus on what matters – the riding itself. Whether you're commuting through Manchester traffic or touring the Scottish Borders, proper insurance means you're protected and legal.

My advice? Don't cheap out on the wrong things. Get proper comprehensive cover if you can afford it, use good security, and be honest on your application. Then forget about the insurance and go ride. Britain has some of the best 125-friendly roads in the world – twisty B-roads through the Yorkshire Dales, coastal routes in Cornwall, mountain passes in Wales – and they're all waiting for you.

Start with our route builder to plan your first proper tour, make sure your insurance paperwork is sorted, and get out there. That's what matters.

Ride safe, and I'll see you on the road.
